title: What randomization actually buys you (and what it doesn’t)
text:
TL;DR — Randomization doesn't remove noise, it removes bias. It makes the treatment independent of the potential outcomes, which is what licenses the difference-in-means as an unbiased effect estimate. Variance is a separate problem — and that's where tricks like CUPED come in.
There’s a common misreading of what an A/B test gives you: the sense that because you randomized, the number you read off is the truth. Randomization is powerful, but it solves exactly one problem — and it’s worth being precise about which one, because the other problems don’t go away.

title: What randomization actually buys you (and what it doesn’t)
section: The setup: two outcomes, one of which you never see
text:
The setup: two outcomes, one of which you never see
For each unit \(i\), imagine two potential outcomes: \(Y_i(1)\) if treated and \(Y_i(0)\) if not. The individual treatment effect is \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\). The catch — the fundamental problem of causal inference — is that you only ever observe one of them:
\[Y_i = T_i \, Y_i(1) + (1 - T_i)\, Y_i(0).\]
So we lower our sights from \(\tau_i\) to the average treatment effect, \(\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]\).

title: What randomization actually buys you (and what it doesn’t)
text:
What randomization does
The natural estimator is the difference in group means. It’s only trustworthy if the treated and control groups would have looked the same absent treatment. Randomization guarantees that by making treatment independent of the potential outcomes:
\[\{Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\} \perp\!\!\!\perp T_i.\]
Under that independence the difference in means is unbiased for the ATE. That’s the whole trick. It’s a statement about bias, not noise.

Randomization buys you exchangeability. It does not buy you precision.

title: What randomization actually buys you (and what it doesn’t)
text:
What it doesn’t do
Your estimate still has variance, and with a skewed metric — revenue, watch-time, anything zero-inflated — that variance can be large enough to hide a real effect. The cheapest fix is CUPED: use a pre-experiment covariate \(X\) correlated with \(Y\) but, by construction, unaffected by treatment, and adjust
\[Y^{\text{cuped}} = Y - \theta\,(X - \bar X), \qquad \theta = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y, X)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.\]
Because \(X\) is independent of treatment, this leaves the estimate unbiased but shrinks its variance by \(1 - \rho^2\), where \(\rho = \operatorname{corr}(Y, X)\). One subtlety worth stating, because it’s easy to get wrong: use a single \(\theta\) and center \(X\) by the pooled mean across both arms. Center each arm by its own mean and the correction cancels out — you get your noisy estimate right back. Let’s see it work:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng  = np.random.default_rng(7)
n, tau, reps, rho = 2000, 0.20, 4000, 0.6   # per-arm N, true effect, sims, corr(X, Y)

def ate_cuped(y_t, y_c, x_t, x_c):
    x = np.concatenate([x_t, x_c]); y = np.concatenate([y_t, y_c])
    theta = np.cov(y, x, ddof=1)[0, 1] / np.var(x, ddof=1)   # pooled slope
    mu_x  = x.mean()                                         # common center (not per-arm!)
    yc_t  = y_t - theta * (x_t - mu_x)
    yc_c  = y_c - theta * (x_c - mu_x)
    return yc_t.mean() - yc_c.mean()

def one_experiment():
    x_t, x_c = rng.normal(size=n), rng.normal(size=n)          # pre-period covariate
    y_t = rho*x_t + np.sqrt(1-rho**2)*rng.normal(size=n) + tau # treated outcome
    y_c = rho*x_c + np.sqrt(1-rho**2)*rng.normal(size=n)       # control outcome
    naive = y_t.mean() - y_c.mean()
    adj   = ate_cuped(y_t, y_c, x_t, x_c)
    return naive, adj

res = np.array([one_experiment() for _ in range(reps)])
naive_sd, cuped_sd = res[:, 0].std(), res[:, 1].std()
print(f"True effect:        {tau:.3f}")
print(f"Naive estimate SD:  {naive_sd:.4f}")
print(f"CUPED estimate SD:  {cuped_sd:.4f}")
print(f"Variance reduction: {100*(1-(cuped_sd/naive_sd)**2):.1f}%   (theory: {100*rho**2:.0f}%)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.hist(res[:, 0], bins=40, alpha=.55, label=f"naive  (SD {naive_sd:.3f})")
ax.hist(res[:, 1], bins=40, alpha=.55, label=f"CUPED (SD {cuped_sd:.3f})")
ax.axvline(tau, color="k", lw=1, ls="--", label="true effect")
ax.set_xlabel("estimated ATE"); ax.set_ylabel("frequency"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

True effect:        0.200
Naive estimate SD:  0.0319
CUPED estimate SD:  0.0259
Variance reduction: 34.2%   (theory: 36%)








Figure 1: Sampling distribution of the ATE estimate over 4,000 simulated experiments. Same unbiased target, much tighter spread once we adjust for a pre-period covariate.





A pre-period metric correlated at \(\rho = 0.6\) cuts variance by about a third — for free, with no extra users and no change to the estimand.

title: What randomization actually buys you (and what it doesn’t)
text:
The takeaway
Keep the two jobs separate. Identification — getting an unbiased target — is what randomization (or a credible quasi-experimental design) handles. Estimation — getting a tight, decision-useful number — is a variance problem you attack with covariate adjustment, stratification, or a better estimator. Conflating them is how teams end up either trusting a noisy readout or blaming randomization for a problem it was never meant to solve.
Next time: what to do when you can’t randomize, and geo-level quasi-experiments become the tool of choice.
